reference.source: GeneReviews MNGIE / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: Suspect MNGIE in a young adult with severe gastrointestinal dysmotility, marked cachexia, ptosis and progressive external ophthalmoplegia, and a peripheral neuropathy
It is an autosomal recessive nuclear disorder caused by mutations in TYMP, which encodes thymidine phosphorylase, leading indirectly to mitochondrial DNA instability

Loss of thymidine phosphorylase activity causes systemic accumulation of thymidine and deoxyuridine, which unbalances the mitochondrial nucleotide pool and produces depletion, deletions and point mutations of mitochondrial DNA
Brain MRI characteristically shows a diffuse, often asymptomatic leukoencephalopathy
Gastrointestinal features (early satiety, dysphagia, gastroparesis, pseudo-obstruction, diarrhoea and diverticulosis) dominate and drive the profound weight loss
Diagnosis is supported by grossly elevated plasma thymidine and deoxyuridine and by low or absent thymidine phosphorylase activity in leucocytes, confirmed by TYMP genetics
Management is largely supportive with nutritional support; disease-modifying strategies that lower toxic nucleosides are handled in specialist centres
reference.pathophysiology: MNGIE is caused by recessive loss-of-function mutations in TYMP, the gene encoding cytosolic thymidine phosphorylase. Without this enzyme, the pyrimidine nucleosides thymidine and deoxyuridine accumulate in blood and tissues. The resulting imbalance of the mitochondrial deoxyribonucleotide pool disturbs mitochondrial DNA replication, causing depletion, multiple deletions and point mutations and thereby a secondary failure of oxidative phosphorylation. The smooth muscle of the gut, peripheral nerves, extraocular muscles and cerebral white matter are particularly affected, producing the visceral myopathy and dysmotility, neuropathy, ophthalmoplegia and leukoencephalopathy that define the disorder.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction from other causes
Anorexia nervosa or other causes of severe cachexia
Coeliac disease and other malabsorptive states
Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia from other mitochondrial causes
additionalInvestigations: Plasma or urine thymidine and deoxyuridine levels, which are markedly elevated
Leucocyte thymidine phosphorylase enzyme activity assay
TYMP molecular genetic testing for confirmation
Nerve conduction studies characterising a demyelinating or mixed neuropathy
Gastrointestinal motility studies and nutritional assessment
redFlags: Intestinal pseudo-obstruction or perforation from diverticular disease
Severe malnutrition and cachexia requiring nutritional rescue
Rapidly progressive neuropathy causing loss of ambulation
reference.prognosis: MNGIE is a progressive, life-limiting disorder; the relentless gastrointestinal dysmotility and cachexia are major contributors to morbidity and premature death, typically in early to mid adulthood without disease-modifying therapy.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the cachexia and gastrointestinal symptoms as an eating disorder or functional gut disorder
Overlooking the diagnosis because the leukoencephalopathy is often clinically silent
Attributing ophthalmoplegia to an isolated ocular myopathy rather than the systemic disease
Not measuring plasma nucleosides, the most accessible and specific biochemical clue
management: Restore thymidine phosphorylase activity to lower toxic thymidine and deoxyuridine, using allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the principal disease-modifying option in selected patients
Consider orthotopic liver transplantation as an alternative enzyme source, or erythrocyte-encapsulated thymidine phosphorylase enzyme replacement where available in trials
Provide aggressive nutritional support, frequently parenteral nutrition, to counter cachexia and intestinal failure
Manage gastrointestinal dysmotility, gastroparesis and pseudo-obstruction with prokinetics, bowel rest and treatment of small-bowel bacterial overgrowth
Give symptomatic care of the peripheral neuropathy, ptosis and ophthalmoplegia
Monitor for and correct nutritional deficiencies and the metabolic consequences of dysmotility
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive TYMP inheritance with family testing
Coordinate care through a specialist mitochondrial and metabolic medicine centre
